_readme: Hand-compiled from web research (see sources per section) on 2026-08-16, checking this site's La Niña regional calls against what actually happened in the 2025-26 Northern Hemisphere season. Not auto-generated — rerun this research manually each summer once a season wraps to keep it current, or ask Claude to redo it.
enso_summary: A weak La Niña: ONI bottomed around -0.61 in Oct–Dec 2025, then faded through neutral by February–March 2026 (ONI -0.21 by JFM). This site's phase-selection logic would have shown "La Niña" content through roughly January, then flipped toward "Neutral" for the back half of the season — a real example of the mid-season phase shifts this site is built to track.

headline_wildcard.title: The March 2026 ridge overrode ENSO across the Interior West
headline_wildcard.text: An exceptional, prolonged ridge centered on Utah and the Great Basin drove the warmest March on record for Colorado (3–4°F above the previous record) and record-high March temperatures across CO/UT/WY. It melted an already-thin snowpack up to 65 days early. April 1, 2026 SWE hit record lows: Colorado 24% of median, Utah 22%, Wyoming 47% — the worst readings since SNOTEL monitoring began in the 1980s. This is exactly the kind of non-ENSO wildcard flagged in the Key Wildcards section below, and it's the single biggest reason this season's actual outcomes diverged from the ENSO-only predictions in the Interior West.

regions.predicted: Bullish (+15–25%) — La Niña's top North American beneficiary
regions.actual: Record December snowfall at Lake Louise, Sunshine, Kicking Horse, and Revelstoke; 80%+ terrain open at Silver Star and Sun Peaks by the holidays.
regions.note: Clean hit, at least for the well-documented early season. No comprehensive late-season recap found for BC specifically to confirm whether the March ridge (which hit the US Interior West hard) also cut into the Canadian Rockies.

regions.actual: Record warmth and a lack of wintry precipitation across the Southwest.
regions.note: One of the cleaner hits this season — the Southwest drought mechanism this site flags as high-conviction played out almost exactly as described.

regions.predicted: Mixed, slightly favorable — La Niña just removes El Niño's headwind rather than creating a strong tailwind
regions.actual: The most impactful winter since 2020-21: a 31" storm Jan 23–27 and a 2–3 foot blizzard Feb 21–23. Real NAO data confirms it ran negative through Dec 2025–Jan 2026 (-0.65, -0.36).
regions.note: Outcome ran better than the modest 'slightly favorable' call — most plausibly because NAO was genuinely negative for the core of the season, reinforcing exactly the mechanism this region's caveat already pointed to. A good example of why the NAO live-check note now appears directly on this region's card.

regions.predicted: Bearish (−10–20%), with an explicit caveat: 'a handful of big atmospheric-river events can still produce an above-average year'
regions.actual: A slow Nov–Dec start (only Mt. Rose/Heavenly open, Mammoth at 30% by mid-Nov), then a holiday storm cycle dumped 4–6 ft, and a Feb 15–20 storm cycle dropped up to 115" near Dodge Ridge.
regions.note: The directional bearish call was too simple on its own, but the caveat written alongside it — boom-or-bust, watch for individual atmospheric rivers — described this exact season almost precisely.

regions.predicted: Bullish (+15–25%) — La Niña's single most reliable US beneficiary
regions.actual: Generally active early season, but Washington's April 1 statewide snowpack came in at just 52% of normal (5th percentile) after the same record-warm March ridge that hit the Interior West.
regions.note: The season likely started consistent with the bullish call, but the March ridge overrode it by spring — a real example of the 'Background Warming / ridging' wildcard beating even a high-conviction ENSO signal.

regions.predicted: Mixed / near average — this site explicitly flags ENSO as having no real predictive power here in any phase
regions.actual: The worst season on record. Salt Lake City had its least snowy winter on record; Colorado's April 1 SWE was 24% of median (less than a third of the prior record low, dating to the 1938-39 Dust Bowl era); Utah came in at 22%.
regions.note: This is the most interesting result of the season: the model correctly refused to credit or blame ENSO for this region, and the actual driver was exactly what an ENSO model can't see — a record-breaking blocking ridge. A historic anomaly happened, and no ENSO-only model, including this one, would have caught it. That's a real limitation worth stating plainly rather than papering over.

regions.predicted: Mixed, elevation-dependent — NAO dominates, not ENSO
regions.actual: No comprehensive season-end recap found; scattered reporting describes an active Atlantic storm track with a favorable negative-NAO window in late Feb–early March.
regions.note: Consistent with the 'NAO matters more than ENSO here' thesis as far as it goes, but I couldn't find hard season-total data to confirm it properly — flagged here rather than overclaiming a hit.

regions.predicted: Bullish — La Niña strengthens the Siberian High, generally the more reliable phase for Japan
regions.actual: Pre-season and mid-season reporting described the 2025-26 season as 'shaping up to be another exceptional year,' consistent with (but not a repeat of) 2024-25's 815cm at Niseko.
regions.note: Available reporting is directionally consistent with the bullish call, but I didn't find a hard final-season snowfall tally to confirm precisely.

regions.predicted: n/a for this backtest — La Niña thesis doesn't apply
regions.note: The Southern Hemisphere 2025 season (Jun–Sep 2025) ran under only a weak, near-neutral ENSO signal (ONI roughly -0.02 to -0.26 through that window), not a real La Niña — so it isn't a fair test of this region's La Niña thesis either way.

regions.predicted: n/a for this backtest — La Niña thesis doesn't apply
regions.note: Same as the Andes: SH 2025 ran ENSO-neutral, not La Niña. See the live validation note below instead — this region's El Niño thesis is being tested in real time this year.

live_validation.title: Right now: Australia's 2026 season under El Niño
live_validation.text: This isn't a backtest — it's happening live. El Niño was officially declared by Australia's Bureau of Meteorology on June 16, 2026. Since then, Australian resorts have recorded one of the warmest mid-winter periods in recent memory: Mt. Hotham, Falls Creek, and Thredbo all logged exceptional July warmth, rain has washed away early snowfall, and the season is tracking below average — precisely the highest-conviction bearish call this site makes for any region in any ENSO phase.

methodology_note: This is a hand-compiled, one-time research pass, not a live-updating scoreboard — the underlying facts (season recaps, snowpack surveys) only exist once a season is basically over. Verdicts are graded against what this site's La Niña content actually claimed, not against a more sophisticated model with the benefit of hindsight. 'Correct for the right reason' is used once, deliberately: Utah/Central Colorado's historic anomaly proves the point this site already made about that region — that ENSO isn't the driver — even though the site's 'near average' language undersold how extreme the actual outcome was.
